name: Irregular Teen Numerative (eleven/twelve)

dimensions.form: Suppletive forms not derived by -teen suffixation

projection.target: Eleven and twelve occupy the first two positions after ten but do not use productive -teen suffixation. Their related ordinals eleventh and twelfth can be compared with thirteenth without analyzing eleven and twelve as -teen stems.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the distinct forms inside the numeral inventory. Current morphological structure is the criterion here.

curious.title: Eleven and twelve
curious.summary: Eleven and twelve sit right after ten, but they aren't built with -teen.
curious.body: Eleven and twelve come right after ten in the counting order, but they don't use the -teen ending that thirteen and the rest use. They're their own forms, not made by adding anything to a single-digit word. This dictionary treats them as separate words with the same jobs as the -teen numbers: in front of a noun, as a multiplier, or added to another number. Their position-words, eleventh and twelfth, can be compared with thirteenth without treating eleven and twelve as -teen words.
curious.try: Count from eleven up to nineteen. Which words don't end in teen?

teacher.summary: Explains eleven and twelve as irregular forms that aren't treated as -teen words.
teacher.explain: Eleven and twelve are suppletive teen numeratives for 11 and 12. They aren't derived by -teen suffixation, though they come in the first two positions after ten. They're lexically atomic and have the same distribution as the regular teens: determiner, factor and addition. Their ordinals eleventh and twelfth can be compared with thirteenth without analyzing eleven and twelve as -teen stems. This dictionary takes current morphological structure as its criterion. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls these forms irregular (in its name for the pattern) and suppletive, not derived by -teen suffixation.
watch_for: A learner might expect eleven and twelve to be built like thirteen, with -teen on a single-digit base.
A learner might think eleven and twelve behave differently from the -teen numbers in a noun phrase, when they have the same distribution.
teacher.activity: Students write the numbers from eleven to nineteen, circle the two that don't end in -teen, and write a short sentence using each of them before a noun.

child.hook: Do eleven and twelve end in teen like thirteen does?
child.explain: Thirteen ends in teen. Eleven and twelve don't. They're special words that don't follow the teen pattern. You use them just like the other numbers.
child.play: Count from eleven up to nineteen out loud. Clap on the two words that don't end in teen.

checked.note: Fixed: the teacher activity and child play said to go from ten to nineteen and pick out the two numbers without -teen, but ten also lacks it; the ranges now start at eleven. Also fixed (unflagged): the same range in the curious try question. Second round: fixed curious.body, which described the factor use as multiplying a larger number (this dictionary sets no size condition); fixed teacher.terms, which called irregular the traditional word and defined suppletive as not derived by -teen, and now gives this dictionary's own wording. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher.summary no longer promises to explain why the forms are irregular.
